title: Sudden Drop
blurb: Tied at four-all with every Pin let go, Dagny has one throw left and a debt that is nearly paid.

blocks.text: "No," I said. "He means me."
Rafe's hand stayed on my arm. He didn't laugh. He went still, the way he goes still when he's the one caught out, and he looked at me as if I were a sum he had got wrong.
"You," he said.

"Since the Coopers. I held their Dropper five minutes in Match 1 and let go the ordinary way, because nobody had taught me any other. Osk named it on the third day. It puts a stone on me every week. I'm carrying seven, near enough. That's why I can't climb."
The Weighman was walking back to his cart as if he had read out a fixture. Nobody else on the Lip said a word. Pru looked at her book and not at Rafe. Osk watched me from his chair, and waited.
"Since my bet," Rafe said. Flat, like a sum read off a slate.
"Since the match."

"Since my bet, Dags. You held him five minutes for my eighty crowns, and I stood on the Lip that night telling jokes about the Coopers' faces, didn't I?" His voice went up at the end the way it always does, and there was nothing under it holding it up.

The coal chit came into my head then, the one with the odds worked out on it that I had left where he would find it, three weeks before Match 1. My throat shut on it. I didn't say it. I am not proud that I kept it back, on that night of all nights, but I did.
"It's not a weight you put on me," I said. "I picked it up."
"What does the plumb-bob do?" He asked it very quietly, very exactly.
"It leans at me from a metre off. Every Anchor on that Lip would see it."
"So you don't stand under it."
"Then I'm treated as found leaning anyway. My fees and my share of the purse go to the league. If I take my name off the register, the same, and the Ninepins don't play the Step."
He took his hand off my arm and put it in his pocket, and took it out again. I loved him so much right then that it hurt under my ribs worse than the knee did.
"There's one way," I said, and I looked at Osk.
He let the quiet go on a long time. Then, low: "Not in front of a Weighman."

"I could throw it on Saturday, in Shaft Nine, with nobody watching but you," I said. "Seven stone is enough behind it. The plumb-bob hangs straight on Monday and I keep my fees. Then we play a Seam side on nulls and Hal's holds and whatever my bones have left, which is three stone before a foot cracks."
"The gate board will have the Colliers odds-on and us at fives against," Pru said. "Six, by Monday."

"Fives against, no purse, and Rafe owes a hundred and twelve on Monday night." I made myself say it plainly, because it was the stake and they needed to hear it. "Or I carry it six more days and throw it in the Step, where it's worth a Drop to us."
"They'll see a Pin set with no hand on it," Osk said. "Every Anchor. The Weighman. The House."
"What does the rulebook say about a Pin set with no hand on it, Pru?"
"Nothing," Pru said. "I've read it end to end for odds. Not a line."
"And Rule 9 wants me found leaning by plumb-bob. After the throw, I won't be."

Osk looked at me a long while. "One," he said. "They'll know what you were. Two: they'll want you more for it, not less." The pause went on so long that Dunnet shifted his feet. "Three: I can't stop you."
"Don't, Dags," Rafe said. "Not for my money. You won't, will you?"
"I'm counted, Rafe," I said, and let it end there.

The Step is played in Shaft Six, on the lower league's field: forty metres to the Throat, six ledges. Its Lip sits in a cut below the Weighhouse yard, and the House runs a cage down to it for the Weighman, his scale and its own people. On Monday I went down in that cage with Rafe, because I could not take the stair. Osk came down after us, chair and all.
The Weighman stood me on the Lip scale before Drop 1. He read the beam, said "Quillon," and wrote five stone in the book.

My bones carried seven. I counted it under my breath while his pencil moved. Ten stone is where a foot cracks. Seven from ten is three. Three stone was all I could lose before my left foot went, and every paid hold would come off it. His stop goes by his book, and his book was two stone light, so he would not stop me until my bones held nearly twelve, two stone past the crack.
Grit on the boards had started to creep toward my boots. I scuffed it flat and stepped off.
The plumb-bob was there already, on a hook on the Weighman's platform rail under a square of sacking, ready for the moment the Step ended. I didn't look at it. I looked at it anyway.
Sibbald Teague stood at the rail beside it in a good grey coat, with his hat in his hand. He inclined his head to me. He didn't need to say the sum. I knew it to the crown, and so did he.
We had the even wall for Drop 1. Lisbet lowered me to L6 in the sling and tied me to the ring of the Pin with a bowline and a half-hitch, and tugged it twice.
"You don't move unless I say move," she said. "And you don't come off my ledge."
Hal went to L4 above me. He put his hand on his strapped side, then on his Pin, and began to hum his one low note.

The Colliers were a Seam side, and they played like one. Their Anchors were a big, slow, exact man called Marr and a narrow one called Ruddock, who turned faster than anyone I had met. Their Dropper was called Kell.
"Evens Marr holds across," Pru called from the Lip, fast and sure. "Seven-to-two he drops it late. Ruddock's the long shot, watch him anyway."
Kell went straight down his rope to the Throat at the bell and stayed there, and I didn't understand why.

I read Marr from the chalk Pru let fall, and set opposite him in the Lap between his ledge and mine, and the Cob hung there between us. That cost nothing. Dunnet hung weightless in the null beside it and reached for it, and his fingers knocked it, and it drifted down out of the Lap into my zone alone.

My set was across at the Colliers' wall, and it took the Cob over and laid it against their wall as if the wall were a floor. Half a head, seven pounds a minute. I held it the whole minute. My left foot took the pounds and told me so.

I couldn't hold it all Drop. When I let go with the Release, the Cob dropped straight down their wall into the Throat, where nobody can set anything, and Kell was under it. That was why. He caught it and carried it across the floor and put it into our well with eighty counts left on the clock.
Colliers three, Ninepins none. Two stone seven between me and a cracked foot.

At the Hoist Dunnet and Rafe winched me to the Lip scale in the sling. Dunnet's face had gone white under the dirt. Rafe, with the rope tails over his shoulder for the swap, saw it and leaned over the edge.

"Their Marr sets so slow, Dunnet, you could go up for your tea and be back on the rope before he's round, couldn't you?" His voice was high and quick. "He was still turning from last week when the bell went, wasn't he?"
Dunnet let out half his big laugh. It wasn't much, but it was something.
I said it before I could think better of it. "And Ruddock turns so fast he leaves the Cob behind him, Dunnet. Stay where he's just been."

Dunnet laughed properly then, and Rafe looked at me, surprised and grateful. It cost me. I had no breath to spare and no laugh in me, and I said it because they both needed to hear me sound like someone who was not afraid. I was afraid of Ruddock. My left foot ached in the boot, and the cold had come into the coat lining and would not go.

Walls swapped. Lisbet took me down to L5 on the odd wall and tied me off. Hal went to L3. The Colliers put Marr on L4, just above me, and Ruddock high on L2, and left L6 true. Pru had priced that before the bell.
"Evens they leave six true," she called. "Evens, and they've done it."
Kell went down to the Throat at the bell again. This time I sent Dunnet down after him.

I nulled Marr in the Lap between his ledge and mine, and for three minutes nothing in that Lap fell. There was nobody in it but the Cob. Then I turned my set a hair off Marr's, and the Cob slid out of the bottom of the Lap into my zone alone, and my set took it across and laid it against the Colliers' wall.

I held it there, seven pounds a minute, while down in the Throat Dunnet and Kell fought shoulder to shoulder for the floor beneath it. I counted the minute out under my breath. My foot told me every pound.

When Dunnet had Kell's back against the slag I let go with the Release, as I do every time now, and my zone went true. The Cob dropped straight down their wall, past L6, which nobody held, into Dunnet's arms. He turned round and put it into their own well.
Three all. Two stone between me and the crack.
Level at the Hoist meant a coin for Drop 3. Pru called it and won it and kept the odd wall.

Drop 3 was the hardest ten minutes I have played. Dunnet came off a rope a body-length from our wall into Ruddock's zone with Ruddock's set already across, and it held him against the stone for sixty counts, and the Colliers had a point. Hal answered it. Kell came off his rope a body-length from his own wall, into Hal's set, and Hal held him there sixty counts, humming. It cost him a stone. I watched it go into his strapped side; his hum broke twice and he picked it up both times. In the last minute, with nobody else in my zone, I held the Cob off our wall, seven more pounds, until the ten-minute bell.
Four all. A stone and seven between me and a cracked foot.
They winched me up for the last Hoist. The Weighman wrote six and a half stone in the book and didn't look up. The Sudden Drop would have no time limit. The first point of any kind would win it.
The coin went up again for walls. Pru called it right again and took the odd wall, because I had asked her to.
I told them on the Lip, low, all of them close round Osk's chair.
"I go to L3, under their L2. Hal, you take L5 and hold true down, whatever happens. I null Marr and keep the Cob above L4 for five minutes, so the Letgo has to be called."
"Then what?" Rafe said.
"Then every Pin is let go for ten counts. Dunnet, at the warning you take the Cob and your rope, and you come down till you're level with my ledge, and you hold it there whatever Kell does."
"Counts," Dunnet said, "I'll hold it till the House pays a fair wage."
"Lisbet. You tie me to the ring and go up onto the rope above me, belayed. When it comes, I'll go out over the shaft. You and the rope hold me."
"I spliced every rope on that wall," Lisbet said. "It'll hold you. Move when I say."
"And at the end of the ten counts I grip the L3 Pin, and throw."
Osk took my good hand in both of his. They were cold.
"One," he said. "Stand. Two: lean out further than you think you can. Three." The pause. "Let go. Little finger last."
Lisbet lowered me to L3 and tied the bowline round my waist and the end round the ring, and went up onto the rope above with a turn round her wrist. I stood in the mark. My knees shook and held.

The Colliers put Marr on L2, just above me, and Ruddock on L4 below, and left L6 true. At the bell Marr set his zone across at our wall. I read him from the chalk and set opposite, and the Cob came down into the Lap between his ledge and mine and stopped dead in the air. Dunnet and Kell drifted into it after it, weightless, grappling. It cost me nothing. It cost Marr nothing.
"Evens they wait you out," Pru called. "Fours they don't."
They waited. So did I. Pru counted the clock down from the Lip, and I counted it under my breath with her, and it was the longest five minutes of my life.
The five-minute bell rang. The Cob was well above the L4 ledge.
"Letgo," the Weighman called. "Three. Two. One."

At the warning Dunnet took the Cob in his left arm and his rope in his right. Kell got onto the next rope over. I let go of my Pin with the Release, and so did every Anchor in the shaft, and the whole of Shaft Six went true down.
Ten counts. Nobody's hand on any Pin.

Dunnet slid down his rope with the Cob, a body-length at a time, until he was level with my ledge, close enough that I could hear him breathing. Kell came down the next rope beside him, snatching at the Cob with his free hand. In true down the Cob dragged at Dunnet's arm like a full bucket. He held it.
"Four," I said. "Five." My right hand was a palm's width from the ring.

Across the shaft Ruddock stood on L4 with his hand above his Pin. He would hold true down when he took it again. True down was all he wanted: the Cob on our wall, and our own well straight beneath it.
"Nine. Ten."
I gripped the L3 Pin.

It was quiet under my hand, quiet as an empty cage. A Pin you have just gripped holds true down until you turn it, so I didn't turn it. I breathed in, all the way. Ruddock gripped his Pin across the shaft, and in the Lap round my ledge his true down added to mine, and Dunnet's arm went down a hand's breadth under the double weight of the Cob. He made a noise in his chest and held on.
I leaned out over the edge of the ledge, out over the shaft, as far as Lisbet's rope would let me, further than I thought I could.
"Cage clear, Da," I said. "Brake off."
I let the breath and the hand go together, little finger last.

Something left me. Not the weight; that stayed in my knees, every pound. It was the pull that had drawn grit and water to my feet since the Coopers, and my body knew it was gone before I did. The ledge went out from under my boots sideways. I went out over the shaft and hung flat out from the wall, and Lisbet's rope took me and held.
The L3 Pin stood alone in its chalk circle with no hand on it, and the whole zone pointed across the shaft, from the Pin through where I had been, at the Colliers' wall.
"Now, Dunnet!"

He let go of the Cob. In the Lap, my set and Ruddock's true down added together, across and down at once, and the Cob went out of Dunnet's arm on a slant and kept going the way it had been sent, down through Ruddock's zone and Hal's and the empty sixth. Ruddock saw it and started his turn. A quarter-turn takes three counts. The Cob took two to reach the Throat. It hit the slag a body's length from the Colliers' wall, bounced once, and went into their well.
I counted the ten on the rope with nobody's hand on my Pin. At ten the zone went true, and I swung in under the ledge and hit the stone with my shoulder, and Lisbet had me before the second swing.
The Weighman's bell rang the Drop. Pru was shouting something from the Lip with no odds in it at all.
Promoted.
They winched me up the moment the Weighman called the inspection. Hal stood under the plumb-bob first, and it hung straight, and he stepped off.
Then me. The Weighman pulled the sacking off the hook. I stood on the chalked spot half a metre from the line, closer than I had ever let myself stand to one, with my knees shaking.
It hung straight. The grit on the boards round my boots stayed where it was.

I was still heavy. The seven stone that had been lean-weight was ordinary carry now, and with what I had paid in the Drops my bones held about eight and a half. But it would drain on any floor in Scarrow, a stone every four hours lying flat, and I could have wept for that alone.
The Weighman wrote in the book. "Sound," he said.
He handed the purse to Pru, because the Caller signs for the side: a hundred crowns in a canvas bag. Pru held it and looked at Hal.
"Give it her," Hal said.
"All of it, Counts," Dunnet said.
"No," I said. "Your mother's rent, Dunnet. Hetty's apprenticeship, Hal. Lisbet, your barge."
"Move your hand," Lisbet said. "It's going in your pocket."
Hal said "Aye," and nothing else, and it was enough.
I let them. Rafe brought the tea tin out of his coat, with the twenty crowns of my fees in it that he had kept for me all season, and counted twelve onto the bag. A hundred and twelve, to the day.

It was the first weight I had ever let anyone else carry for me. I said so, out loud, to all of them, and then I cried, on the Lip of Shaft Six with the Weighman watching. I didn't put my face in the coat. My throat hurt with it and my eyes ran and I let them. I loved them, every one, and for once I said that too.
Rafe took the bag to the rail and put it into Sibbald Teague's hands.

Teague counted it, taking his time. "One hundred and twelve," he said. "To the day, Rafe Quillon." He looked past Rafe at me, and then down the shaft at the L3 Pin. "It would have been a shame, Dagny Quillon." He put on his hat and rode the cage up to the yard.
My fingers found the stitched square in the coat lining, at my left hip, where they always find it now. The stiff corner of the paper was still there. I didn't open it.
The Weighman closed the book.
"Miss Quillon."
I turned round.
"The plumb-bob's straight," he said. "I've written it. Your fees and your share stand." He tapped the book against his palm. "But only a leaning Anchor sets a Pin without a hand, Miss Quillon."
Behind him the cage came down from the yard, and the gate slid back.
Rafe knew her before I did. "That's the Settle's matron," he said, under his breath. "Farrant. Ide Farrant."
She wore the Settle's grey, and she stepped out of the lift cage onto the Lip as if she had been sent for.
"A girl who can lean, throw, and walk out of the shaft," Matron Ide Farrant said. "The Settle will see you now."
